lesson.title: Leapfrogging Toward Japan
lesson.summary: In the vast Pacific theater, American commanders adopted an island hopping strategy, seizing selected strategic islands while bypassing heavily fortified Japanese strongholds, to advance steadily toward Japan itself.
lesson.body:
The war against Japan that began with the U.S. entry into World War II presented a very different challenge than the war in Europe. Rather than a single continuous front, the Pacific theater was an ocean dotted with thousands of islands, many held by Japanese forces who had fortified them heavily after years of expansion. Attacking every Japanese-held island directly would have been slow and enormously costly in lives. American commanders instead developed a strategy often called island hopping, or leapfrogging: capturing selected islands that offered strategically useful airfields or harbors, while deliberately bypassing and isolating other, more heavily defended islands, cutting them off from supplies and reinforcement rather than assaulting them outright.

Two major American commanders led parallel drives across the Pacific. Admiral Chester Nimitz directed a Central Pacific campaign, pushing through island chains such as the Gilbert and Mariana Islands, while General Douglas MacArthur led a Southwest Pacific campaign advancing through New Guinea and back toward the Philippines, which he had been forced to retreat from in 1942 while promising, 'I shall return.' The two campaigns often converged on the same objectives from different directions, gradually squeezing Japan's defensive perimeter.

Key battles marked the strategy's progress. The long, grinding fight for Guadalcanal in 1942 and early 1943 marked the first major American offensive of the Pacific war. Later battles at islands including Tarawa, Saipan, Guam, Peleliu, Iwo Jima, and Okinawa were often extraordinarily bloody, since Japanese forces frequently fought to near annihilation rather than surrender, and by 1944 and 1945 increasingly used kamikaze suicide attacks against American ships. The capture of the Mariana Islands in 1944 proved especially significant, since it put American long-range B-29 bombers within striking distance of the Japanese home islands for the first time.

By early 1945, island hopping had brought American forces to Iwo Jima and then Okinawa, both close enough to Japan that the fighting there offered a grim preview of what a full invasion of the Japanese home islands might cost in casualties on both sides. That sobering experience weighed heavily on American planning for how to bring the war to an end without such an invasion.
